reason: The Royal Commission report and a separately written engineering history support the retained claims; see the linked scan for exact finding (j) wording.
story: On August 27, 1907, the bend in lower chord 9-L of the unfinished Quebec Bridge was found to have greatly increased. Bridge staff measured deflections and discussed their danger. On August 29, the bridge collapsed over the St. Lawrence River. The Royal Commission found that defective lower-chord design caused the collapse. It did not believe action after August 27 could have prevented the fall, but said better judgment by those responsible might have prevented the loss of life.
angle: The inquiry distinguished the doomed structure from the lives that might have been saved; show the reported warning, the collapse, and the commission’s conditional finding without inventing a stop-order counterfactual.

claims.claim: Some workers considered the bending critical, while Superintendent Birks believed there was no danger and that the bend had always been present.

evidence.quote: Mr. Birks expressed himself definitely as being of opinion that there was no danger, and endeavoured to persuade me that the bend had always been in the chord. Mr. Yenser and I were uneasy

Some of the Phoenix Bridge men on the job, including Yenser, the foreman, believed the situation was critical. Birks, the Superintendent, continued to believe the bend was in the member from the beginning.

disputed: The origin of the bends in the lower chords: inspectors on site argued that the bends occurred after erection due to stress from the growing weight, while Phoenix Bridge officials and designer Birks argued the bends had been present in the chord before shipping or were made in the shop. The script should explain that while workers on-site recognized the danger of buckling under weight, corporate management tried to dismiss it as a pre-existing manufacturing flaw.
